questions.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,-(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})) \\  & \,\,=-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{a}_{n}=\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}-{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=2,$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=1.
$$

Next, from the third equation, ${b}_{n}=-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}.$ Substituting this into the third equation, gives

$$
(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2})\frac{n\pi }{2}-{a}_{n}=\frac{4}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}.
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{2}\cdot (-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}) \\  & =\frac{8}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼1 & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{8}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,-3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,=-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-2 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=0 \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n}=\frac{6}{n\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=\frac{4}{3},$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Next, from the second equation, ${b}_{n}=\frac{9{a}_{n}}{n\pi }.$ Substituting this into the third equation, gives

$$
-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3(\frac{9{a}_{n}}{n\pi })=\frac{6}{n\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{18}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81}.
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{9{a}_{n}}{n\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{n\pi }\cdot (-\frac{18}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81}) \\  & =-\frac{162}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼\frac{2}{3} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{18}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{162}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)) \\  & \,+5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({b}_{n}n\pi +5{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-{a}_{n}n\pi +5{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).\end{aligned}

$$

{\begin{aligned}-12\pi A=0 \\ 12\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{108\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{108\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\pi A=0 \\ \pi B=6\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{6}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving First Order ODEs Given the Fourier Series of the Forcing Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Fourier series of a particular solution of the differential equation

$$
y'-2y=f(x),
$$

where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x) \sim 3 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{12}{n^2\pi}\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right).
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We assume that a particular solution has the following Fourier series:

$$
y_p \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right) + b_n \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for $y'_p$ and $y_p$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,-2(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,=3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & -{a}_{0}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,=3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{a}_{0}=3 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{a}_{n}=\frac{12}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-2{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation,

$$
a_0=-3,
$$

which means the constant term is

$$
\dfrac{a_0}{2}=-\dfrac{3}{2}.
$$

Next, from the third equation,
$b_n=-\dfrac{a_n n\pi}{6}.$
Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
\left(-\dfrac{a_n n\pi}{6}\right)\dfrac{n\pi}{3}-2a_n=\dfrac{12}{n^2\pi}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
a_n=-\dfrac{216}{n^2\pi(n^2\pi^2+36)}.
$$

Therefore, for $b_n$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{6} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{6}\cdot (-\frac{216}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}) \\  & =\frac{36}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼-\frac{3}{2} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{216}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{36}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Second Order ODEs Given the Fourier Series of the Forcing Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Fourier series of a particular solution of the differential equation $y''-y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x) \sim 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^3\pi} \sin(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: We may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Because the forcing function has only a constant term and sine terms, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for $y''_p$ and $y_p$ into the equation and have

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty -b_n n^2\pi^2 \sin(n\pi x)
-
\left( \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n \sin(n\pi x) \right)
=
1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^3\pi} \sin(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get

$$
-\dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n(-n^2\pi^2-1)\sin(n\pi x)
=
1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^3\pi} \sin(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y_p \sim 
-1
+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \:
\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^3\pi(n^2\pi^2+1)}
\cdot
\sin(n\pi x).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation $y'' + 9\pi^2 y = f(x),$ where the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n^2}\sin(n\pi x).
$$

What harmonic of the forcing function does the natural frequency of the system match?
And what is the resonant component of a particular solution?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation

$$
y''+9\pi^2 y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of

$$
\omega=\sqrt{9\pi^2}=3\pi.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $\left(L=1\right)$ are

$$
\omega_n=\dfrac{n\pi}{1}=n\pi.
$$

For $n=3$, we have $\omega_3=3\pi.$ Since $\omega_3=\omega,$ the natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function. This is the answer to the first question.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
f_3(x)=\dfrac{1}{9}\sin(3\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
y_{p_3}=x(A\cos(3\pi x)+B\sin(3\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))+x(-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for $y''_{p_3}$ and $y_{p_3}$ into the equation $y''+9\pi^2 y=\dfrac{1}{9}\sin(3\pi x){:}$

$$
\left[-6\pi A\sin(3\pi x)+6\pi B\cos(3\pi x)-9\pi^2 y_{p_3}\right]+9\pi^2 y_{p_3}=\dfrac{1}{9}\sin(3\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-6\pi A\sin(3\pi x)+6\pi B\cos(3\pi x)=\dfrac{1}{9}\sin(3\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14074986/assets/599de8dda7f476da630651310a373eae36280c75676a44da91105c9a1751456b.png)

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
y_{p_3}=-\dfrac{x}{54\pi}\cos(3\pi x).
$$
